title: Chevron stitch
subtitle: A zig-zag border stitch worked between two parallel lines with a back stitch at each peak
excerpt: Chevron stitch creates an even zig-zag band between two parallel guide lines. The needle takes a small back stitch at each upper and lower point of the zig-zag, then travels diagonally to the opposite line. The result is a continuous linked zig-zag with small horizontal bars at the peaks, used for borders, smocking and geometric band designs.
sourceNotes: Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), border and line stitches sections (Project Gutenberg #20776). Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882).

glossaryTerms.definition: The drawn or traced line on the fabric that guides where the stitches go.

content.text: Chevron stitch is a geometric border stitch worked between two parallel

. It travels diagonally from the bottom line to the top line and back, taking a small back stitch at each peak to produce a horizontal bar. The resulting band is a continuous linked zig-zag with neat bars at each turning point. Chevron stitch is used for decorative borders, geometric samplers, smocking on fabric, and as a filling when rows are worked close together to form a diamond grid.

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Medium-weight cotton or linen; even-weave fabric helps keep spacing regular

content.text: Draw or trace two parallel horizontal lines roughly 1 cm apart. Mark equal intervals of about 5 mm along each line to act as stitch guides. The stitch is worked from left to right.

Secure the thread and bring the needle up at point A on the bottom line. Insert it down at point B, 5 mm to the right on the same (bottom) line. Come back up at point C, midway between A and B on the bottom line (that is, 2 to 3 mm back from B). Pull through. This is the first back stitch bar on the bottom line.

From point B, take the needle diagonally up to the top line. Insert it down at point D on the top line and come back up at point E, 5 mm to the right of D on the top line. Pull through. This is the diagonal leg rising to the top line.

At the top line, work the back stitch bar: insert the needle down at point D again (going back into the same hole) and come up at point F, 5 mm further right along the top line. This creates the horizontal bar at the upper peak.

From point F, take the needle diagonally back down to the bottom line. Insert it down 5 mm to the right on the bottom line and come back up midway between, as in step 2. Work the back stitch bar at the lower peak.

Continue alternating: diagonal up, back stitch bar at top, diagonal down, back stitch bar at bottom. Keep the diagonal legs at the same angle and the bars the same length throughout. At the end of the row, fasten off on the back.

items.cause: Inconsistent spacing along the guide lines
items.fix: Mark the intervals before you start and keep them equal on both lines. On plain-weave fabric, counting threads gives the most reliable spacing.

items.symptom: The horizontal bars at the peaks are missing or very small
items.cause: The back stitch at each peak is being skipped or made too short
items.fix: At each peak, the needle must go back into the hole it just exited (or the interval start) and come out at the next interval mark. This back stitch is what forms the visible bar and links the diagonal legs.

items.symptom: The thread crosses under the fabric in long diagonal runs, pulling the fabric
items.cause: Carrying the thread across the back rather than working it through the fabric
items.fix: The diagonal leg of chevron stitch does cross on the back; this is normal. Keep the back floats short by using the correct stitch length (5 to 8 mm is typical). Very long stitch intervals produce long back floats.
